query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, high-temperature stable Al2O3 ceramic coating via chemical vapor deposition on as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will create an adherent, self-healing oxygen barrier that significantly improves oxidation resistance during prolonged exposure at ≈1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere, while preserving the intrinsic room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa) of the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with known ductility at room temperature and yield strength at high temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin Al2O3 coating using chemical vapor deposition.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air) for extended periods (tens to hundreds of hours) and mechanical loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹ during high-temperature testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The conformal, thin ceramic interface layer created by the Al2O3 coating.
generation.mechanism: The ceramic coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy, thereby reducing oxidation and preserving the microstructural integrity that governs mechanical properties. Its self-healing nature under thermal cycling further ensures continued protection without altering the alloy’s intrinsic ductility or yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated samples will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation (lower weight gain and reduced oxygen penetration) after prolonged high-temperature exposure, while retaining room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength comparable to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-cast alloy showing poor oxygen resistance despite having 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: The intervention is designed for conditions around 1000 °C under oxidizing environments with strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹; its effect on other temperature regimes or mechanical loading conditions remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding long-term adhesion and potential thermal stress effects of the coating during cyclic temperature changes, which could indirectly affect the alloy’s mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr with the deposited thin Al2O3 coating via CVD, and a control group of untreated as-cast samples. Expose both groups to 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) for 100 hours. After exposure, perform weight gain measurements, cross-sectional microscopy to assess oxygen penetration, and mechanical tensile tests (at room temperature and at high temperature using strain rates within 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Mass change (weight gain) due to oxidation.
Oxygen concentration depth profile in the alloy (using EDS or SIMS).
Tensile stress-strain curves to determine yield strength and ductility at room and high temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (lower weight gain and oxygen penetration) compared to the control, or if their mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) degrade noticeably relative to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
